en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Bīlíng during the Táng Dynasty.
The following section explains the meaning of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* through the lens of the *Nirvāṇa*.

While the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is scattered throughout various teachings, no other scripture provides such detailed and comprehensive definitions and characteristics as this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Therefore, the fourfold and sixfold formulations are cited here for explanation.

The meaning of non-arising is that there is no arising whatsoever— neither from self nor other, neither wisdom nor the objects of abandonment, neither phenomena nor principle, nor the conceivable nor the inconceivable.
All are non-arising.
This refers to the meaning of "illuminating and manifesting" through cause and effect;
it is found throughout the nineteenth sutra.
First, regarding the explanation of the four phrases, the first phrase is "hearing what has not been heard."
Regarding the various meanings:
at the beginning of the sutra, four propositions are listed, starting with "not hearing what has been heard" and so forth;
next, four propositions are presented, starting with "the unarisen arising" and so forth.
He explains "not hearing what is heard" and so forth;
furthermore, he explains "not arising what arises" and so forth by means of the four propositions, such as "not reaching what is reached."
Therefore, it is said that "not hearing yet hearing" and so forth have various meanings.
Now, speaking from the middle way and in accordance with non-arising (*anutpāda*),
we employ "the arising of the unarisen" and so forth to explain the meaning of non-arising.
However, the ancients placed the four phrases—“hearing what is unheard,” “giving birth to what is unborn,” and so forth—at the beginning.
Each subsequent phrase merely serves as a further explanation of them;
therefore, they mostly provide exegeses for these four phrases, such as “hearing what is unheard.”
The remaining phrases are merely illustrative examples.
Some say that hearing and not hearing are simultaneously the conventional and the ultimate.
"Not hearing what is heard" is both the ultimate and the conventional;
"hearing what is heard" is merely the conventional;
"not hearing what is not heard" is merely the ultimate.
It is further said:
"Not hearing yet hearing" arises from the True as a response;
"hearing yet not hearing" gathers the response back into the Source.
"Not hearing" means that the Dharma-body is quiescent;
"hearing and hearing" refers to the unceasing manifestation of responsive traces.
Regarding "not arising yet arising," and so forth, there have been many interpretations since antiquity.
Xinghuang explained this using the Snow Mountain verse:
"That which is not born from birth is the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena;
that which is born from non-birth is the nature of arising and ceasing."
"Arising after arising is birth; when extinction is extinguished, there is no further arising.
This non-arising is the bliss of quiescent extinction.
Furthermore, this is explained by means of the four verses on transcendence.
Regarding the "four exits," this verse emerges from four locations.
The ancients named them the "four pillars of nirvāṇa," namely [the verses] numbered ninety-five,
twenty-five, twenty-six, and [twenty-seven].
The non-arising of arising is that which was originally non-existent but now exists;
the arising of non-arising is that which was originally existent but now no longer exists.
That the arising of arising exists as a dharma throughout the three periods of time, while the non-arising of non-arising does not exist at all—such a state of affairs is impossible.
It further states:
"The Tathāgata realizes nirvāṇa," and so forth, correlating these with the four propositions.
Zhan’an said:
As stated below: "Because of this matter, I immediately attained understanding of a single phrase or half-phrase;
I beheld the Buddha-nature and entered nirvana.
One should know that these are all phrases for beholding the Buddha-nature.
The nature of the definitive cause for hearing what has not been heard;
the nature of the conditional cause for not hearing what has been heard;
and the nature of the primary cause for neither hearing nor not hearing.
The nature of the object of hearing and hearing can be used as an analogy to explain "non-arising arising" and so forth;
this should likewise be understood.
Although many ancient commentators have offered explanations, none have yet fully grasped the essential purport of the sutra.
According to Zhanran’s interpretation, this is but one approach; Zhanran states:
"None of these [views] are correct; in this wisdom, both the cause and fruit of severance are non-arising."
However, for the purpose of explaining this sūtra, a separate approach has been made. In that sūtra,
when the Buddha wished to speak of these matters— such as "hearing what is unheard" and so forth—
he emitted light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha from the eastern quarter.
When he first arrived,
the entire great assembly perceived what was not blue as blue.
Even those who perceive what is not white as white and so forth—
when the bodhisattvas and others behold this light,
they all ask one another:
"What light is this?
They all remained silent and did not answer.
He then questioned Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Radiance is itself wisdom;
wisdom is itself the eternally abiding."
"Even this is the Tathāgata; even this is great compassion.
The Buddha said, "Do not now enter the samādhi of the profound ultimate truth."
This should be explained according to conventional truth.
Mañjuśrī said:
"To the east of here, beyond twenty Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a world named Pūrṇacandra."
In that world there was a bodhisattva named Vaidūryaprabha.
Seeing the light there, he questioned that Buddha,
and the Buddha replied:
To the west, at a distance of twenty times the sands of the Ganges from here, there is a world named Sahā.
The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni,
who preaches for the sake of all bodhisattvas such as "hearing what has not been heard" and so forth.
That bodhisattva addressed that Buddha, saying:
"I wish to come here to hear what has not been heard and so forth;
before departing from there, these signs have first appeared here."
If the various Śākyas of antiquity each followed their own single path,
by what means could they have manifested the intent of the "Summoning of Light," and by what means could they have given rise to the great doubts of those throughout the ten directions?
I fear that I may have failed to honor the command sent by that Buddha;
how could this possibly suffice to repay his sentiments for coming from so far away?

Herein, the sutra is interpreted to explain the meaning of "non-arising" (*wusheng*).
Therefore, following the sequence of the scriptural text,
first the four propositions are listed;
next, below this, the characteristics of inclusion are briefly set forth.

Abiding in the stage of Sublime Enlightenment,

"First, 'the arising of the non-arising' refers to the first phrase of the sūtra;

Now, the commentary by the Great Master is explained below.
Because he wishes to clarify that which is established, he first explains conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
because he next clarifies that which establishes, he subsequently explains abiding therein.
In principle, they are fundamentally non-dual, being neither conjoined nor separate.
Yet, in terms of phenomena, it is provisionally said that ignorance is "conjoined" with them;
the same applies to the producer and the produced, as well as the stabilizer and the stabilized.
Because it is stabilized by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) then becomes the inconceivable object.
Stabilization is precisely *vipaśyanā*.
When this *vipaśyanā* first attains its name, it is called the stage of practice through contemplation (*vipaśyanā-caryā-bhūmi*).
By means of the understanding of perfect contemplation, one entrusts oneself to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This contemplation is the "sacred gestation.
Because the sacred one entrusts itself to the womb, it is called "entrusting oneself to the sacred womb" (*āryagarbha-pratiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, being born within the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) is called "entrusting oneself to the noble womb" (āryagarbha).
Entering the first stage (prathamavihāra) is called "emerging from the noble womb.
Because the noble ones emerge from the womb, it is termed "emerging from the noble womb."
Because it arises from the noble ones, it is called "emerging from the womb of the noble ones.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that introduces the citation from the scripture as proof:
All phenomena are themselves ignorance, which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The arising of *prajñā* is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This concludes the exposition below by way of demonstration.
The phrase "explaining non-arising and non-ceasing" below reiterates the second clause.
Next, the passage following "non-arising and non-ceasing" provides the scriptural explanation.
The term "Great Nirvana" serves as the general heading.
The section on the characteristic of arising explains the two types of non-arising.
Because the characteristic of arising is exhausted, the virtue of wisdom and abandonment is fulfilled.
Because it is attained through the path of cultivation, it clarifies that the fruit accords with its cause.
Now, following the explanation of the Great Master,
the two virtues are already perfected, which explains that the marks of arising have been exhausted;
this refers directly to wondrous enlightenment as the fruit of quiescent extinction.
The section on cause and effect concludes with the "Buddha-treasury" (buddhagarbha).
"Conclusion" (jie) means to tie together as one.
In the commentary on the sutra, the third phrase is listed below.
The preceding section is an exegesis on the conventional truth (*saṃvṭi-satya*).
The following section is the Great Master’s commentary.
Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), it unites with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to give rise to all dharmas.
Therefore, ignorance is named as the root.
By merely destroying this root, all phenomena do not arise;
"death" is simply another name for this non-arising.
This commentary further clarifies the intended meaning of this phrase below.
By means of this virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), it explains the initial virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*);
for if there were no virtue of abandonment, the virtue of wisdom would not be accomplished.
Therefore, one must explain wisdom (jñāna) by means of the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa).
If the virtue of wisdom is accomplished in the first phrase, it constitutes the "inferior" character in that first phrase;
if the virtue of abandonment is accomplished in this [second] phrase, [it constitutes the "superior" character].
In this very phrase, the term "non-arising" (anutpāda) at the end refers to what is called "equality" (samatā);
it serves to distinguish [this] from the term "non-arising" found in the two preceding phrases.
In the first phrase, the term "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) is applied above;
in this phrase, it is applied below.
Although the names in both instances refer to the same phenomenon, their underlying principles differ.
The first phrase concerns the virtue of wisdom that takes principle as its object; it is called "non-arising.
This phrase destroys the delusions regarding phenomena until they are exhausted, thereby attaining the name "non-arising.
When viewed from the perspective of principle toward phenomena, phenomena are considered inferior.
Therefore, it is said that the lower [level] is "broken.
Since the principle (li) is superior when viewed from the perspective of phenomena (shi),
it is called the "superior object-condition" (shang-yuan).
Next, beneath the first phrase, the two instances of the character "sheng" (arising) within the two phrases are distinguished.
The "sheng" beneath the first phrase belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*);
the "sheng" above this phrase belongs to affliction (*kleśa*).
Although the term "birth" (*jāti*) occurs in both places and its name is the same,
the "birth" in the first phrase belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*), and wisdom is itself liberation (*vimukti*).
The "birth" in this [second] phrase belongs to affliction (*kleśa*), and affliction is itself bondage (*bandhana*).
Therefore, it is said that there is a great difference.
Since both cases involve both arising and non-arising,
one must distinguish them as being identical in name but different in meaning.
Since the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment have no sequence of priority,
if the third [virtue] can explain the first,
the first may likewise explain the third.
This is because wisdom and abandonment occur simultaneously.
Although their essence is non-dual, one must first employ wisdom in order to abandon delusion;
how could delusion be abandoned on its own before wisdom arises?
Therefore, let us first use the third [explanation] to explain the first.
Furthermore, even if the third were placed at the beginning,
the first could likewise be used to explain the third.
I shall not burden you with further writing and will follow the sequence of the text.
Furthermore, it is simply because this follows from the meaning that it is so.

the conclusion likewise connects by identifying it with the characteristics of the first phrase;

Therefore, it is said that "at one time" cannot be [divided into] before and after; this is the re-explanation based on the scripture below.

The preceding and following sections of the sutra explain these two meanings—*svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and *vibhāga* (differentiation).
Therefore, the Great Master here judges and distinguishes the differing characteristics of these two passages.
The "former" refers to the previous interpretation.
Since it was stated that "the virtue of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) signifies the extinction of the delusions of one's own practice,
this section provides a further explanation by specifying that these refer to the four abodes of the bodhisattvas.
This means that once a bodhisattva has severed the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), they are able to manifest births with mastery.
Having first severed the four abidings— just as a bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-yāna*) does—
they are already able to benefit sentient beings with mastery.
How much more so when entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), where the true cause is distinguished:
by means of the inferior severance of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*) by those of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*),
the superior severance of the five abidings (*pañca-vāsa*) by those of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*) is revealed.
Regarding "the extinction of delusion" (*moha-nirodha*) below, the Buddha-treasury (*buddhagarbha*) is again used to conclude the two interpretations.

"The extinction of delusion" clarifies "spitting out" (*niṣṭhīvana*) to conclude the primary explanation, while "the arising of transformation" (*nirmāṇa-samudaya*) clarifies "blowing away" (*pradhūpana*) to conclude the secondary explanation.
"The scriptural explanation" below cites the fourth phrase of the sutra.
"Everything below [the phrase] 'the sutra explains' is the Master’s commentary.

The section beginning with 'for what purpose does the bodhisattva' below restates the previous point for further explanation."
One considers this to be capable of transformation.

because its continuity is uninterrupted, it is called "birth-of-birth" (jāti-jāti).
"Life after life" refers to the realm of those to be transformed.

This is for the purpose of establishing the capacity for non-arising (*anutpāda*) as the final bond.
The preceding three phrases all constitute the capacities for transforming others. [These comprise] the knowledge of cause and effect, and the abandonment [of afflictions].

Regarding the four abodes (*vihāra*) mentioned below, the Great Master again uses the four abodes from the sixth abode of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* to explain the Buddha’s repeated explanation of the bodhisattvas of the four abodes.
The sixth stage of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* corresponds precisely to this distinct meaning.
Since even the Buddha previously manifested the perfect and superior by means of the common and inferior,

therefore, I cite it to clarify that the "sixth dwelling" (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*) mentioned in the *Yuanmiao lun* refers to the point from the tenth dwelling onward where one first receives the name of a "dwelling."
Regarding the phrase "if a person lacks the seed-nature (gotra)," this refers to bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith;
thus it says, "although born in the good realms," and so forth.
As for "not being among the number of those in the six ranks," [it means they have not yet entered the stage of the true lineage].
This is because these are not subsumed within the six stages of abiding (*vihāra*).
Since these six types of persons are all non-retrogressive,
they are termed "abidings."
Furthermore, it is said that "ultimate" refers to the exhaustion of the Bodhisattva stages,
not eternal ultimacy.
The accomplishment of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is the fulfillment of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*).
Because they have already severed both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it is said that there is no regression.
"Attained by one person" refers to the first of the six [types of practitioners].
Furthermore, even those who are practicing toward [the goal] do so by means of abiding within these stages.
Only after severing the views and afflictions can one proceed;
therefore, it is said that one "progresses repeatedly.

but rather because those stages are still far removed.

it is called "skillful means.
As for "the pure mind being the first bhūmi":

As for "traversing the traces of the path":
The stage of cultivating the distinct path refutes the thought of identity;
the stage of ultimate certainty refutes both thoughts together.
The Sūtra is cited below as the basis for the treatise’s interpretation of the Sūtra.
Reaching the traces of the Path is called "truly emerging from the conventional.
Because it is taught as a path that carries [the provisional] with it, the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa) are established;
when one reaches this stage through the gradual [path], it can still bring great benefit.
How much more so for one who has exhausted the five stages in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
and how much more so for one who has perfected the integration of wisdom and the severance of afflictions?
The sutra next explains the six phrases in sequence.
The reason the Sūtra reiterates the six propositions is that the preceding four propositions directly clarify that cause and effect, as well as subject and object, are non-arising.
Although the very term "non-arising" is itself a negation, [the Sūtra further clarifies this].
Since non-arising has not yet been refuted,
it is therefore clarified here that all are inexpressible.
Furthermore, although the first four propositions speak of non-arising, [they do not fully capture its nature].
Since it is not yet known what kind of non-arising this is,
within these six propositions, both the conceivable and the inconceivable—
both arising and non-arising— are entirely refuted.
Therefore, all six propositions are inexpressible;
this reveals the primary intent of the current text’s universal refutation.
First, the six propositions are correctly explained as being inexpressible to clarify the practice for oneself (*svayam-ācāra*).
Among these, first the scriptural passages are listed;
following this, the meaning of the passages is briefly explained.

The fact that the phrase "inexpressible" appears under each and every clause signifies the sense of refutation;
the initial passage provides a brief determination of this.
Regarding the phrase "conceptual and non-conceptual delusions," it should have been stated as "conceptual and non-conceptual delusions and their antidotes.
In the text, for the sake of brevity, only "delusions" is mentioned.
To understand and resolve doubts sequentially is the conceivable;
to understand and resolve doubts non-sequentially is the inconceivable.
Understanding is that which can destroy [delusion].
Delusion is that which is to be destroyed;
therefore, delusion and awakening follow one another in their characteristics,
and are thus collectively termed "conceivable and inconceivable."
Both delusion and liberation must be universally refuted;
one cannot even speak of them as "inconceivable," let alone as "conceivable."
Therefore, beneath each and every phrase, it is said that they are "unspeakable.
Question:
Since conceptual thought must be shattered, what is the use of shattering the inconceivable?
Answer:
Because their principles are neither universal nor perfect, all must be refuted.
If one refutes the perfect, it is to refute the perfect as distinct from the partial.
Because it does not contradict the perfect principle, it is said that the nirvāṇa attained within the minds of the sages is not refuted;
however, it is refuted because those who have not yet attained it cling to it and thereby produce frivolous conceptual proliferation (prapañca). Therefore, it is refuted.
What follows is the sub-commentary.
First, it explains the four propositions regarding the conceptualization of delusion and awakening;
therein, it first refutes delusion.
Next, the refutation.
Regarding the first delusion, there are two phrases.
First, the explanation establishes that it is inconceivable.
Next, the explanation establishes that [the nature of reality] is inexpressible.
Regarding the first phrase, "afflictions outside the realm":
while the principle-nature is non-arising, afflictions are arising.
Therefore, it is said that "non-arising gives rise.
The delusions within the realm [of desire] are called "branches and tips," whereas the delusions outside the realm have already arisen.
From the arising of delusion, further delusion arises;
hence it is called "arising of arising.
That which is outside the realms is precisely the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The "within the realm" refers to the delusions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa).
Because they possess both coarse and subtle aspects, and because they are categorized as internal and external,
they are judged to be delusions that are conceivable.
This section below demonstrates the characteristic of mutual dependence.
First, it clarifies that "arising from arising" (*jātijāti*) is the objective realm of those to be converted.
As for the term "simultaneous" (*saha*):
Since all that is produced is a transformation,
they are mutually dependent by virtue of their causal capacities.
Since that which is transformed cannot be apprehended, it is subsequently explained as being "inexpressible."
It is explained that both the transformer and the transformed are ineffable,
just as a phantom person preaches the Dharma to another phantom person.
Question:
Since that which is capable of transformation is a distinct affliction,
why is it called "sovereign"?
Answer:
Having already severed the pervasive afflictions,
one is said to possess mastery over them;
yet, regarding the specific afflictions, one remains bound.
The branches and the root are both the dharma-nature;
by contemplating this dharma-nature, one transcends delusion,
which is termed "ineffable."
Next, as for the refutation below, which refutes the notion of "conceivable understanding," it first explains the two lines to establish them as being conceivable,

Regarding the statement that the explanations outside the [three] realms "dualistically dispel," this derives its name from what precedes it; furthermore,

One should say that it is the destruction of delusions;

Because delusions are destroyed, birth and death are necessarily destroyed.
By destroying the delusions within the realm of desire, one causes them not to arise;
hence it is said, "arising and non-arising."
Question:
Since the delusions outside the realm are capable of transformation,
what is the difference between them and the liberation within the realm?
Answer:
Liberation within the realm [of existence] breaks the afflictions within the realm;
thus, it receives the name "liberation."
Having already been fully bound within that external realm,
it is called an "external defilement" (*bāhyakleśa*).
Although it is designated as a defilement according to its specific category, it is capable of transforming the defilements within the internal realm.
Although their substance is not distinct, they receive different names because their locations differ.
This interpretation below demonstrates the aspect of mutual dependence;
it is called "various" because there are sixteen different gates.
From the shallow to the profound, all belong to the stage of self-cultivation;
as for the sequence of preceding and succeeding stages and the position of transforming others,
these are explained in relation to the four teachings.
Thus, multiple types of differing causes and effects are established,
as explained in the first fascicle within the section on the Four Great Vows.
Even the principle of "the inferior cannot explain" remains beyond description.
The fourfold Truth of the Path is that which leads to the goal;
the principle of cessation, the dharma-nature, is that which is to be reached.
Since even the substance of this principle does not exist, how could there be various things that lead or that are led?
Therefore, all [of these] are inexpressible.
Next, in the refutation of the inconceivable, there is first delusion and then understanding.
This delusion and understanding merely point to ignorance in contrast to the perfect principle.
Without distinguishing between internal and external, branches and roots,
it is therefore called "inconceivable.
Within the initial refutation of delusions, one first explains and establishes its inconceivability.
Therefore it is said that it is merely ignorance.
Ignorance cannot be apprehended; below this, it is explained that it is ineffable.
That which cannot be apprehended is precisely what is ineffable.
Next, regarding the refutation of the inconceivable understanding:
it first demonstrates the characteristics of the inconceivable;
therefore, it is said that this is simply the perfect understanding.
Within this, the perfect cause and perfect fruit are established.
As for the principle that it is not partial or perfect, the following clarifies that it is ineffable:
because the principle is not partial, it cannot be explained in a partial manner.
Since the principle is not yet complete, how can it be explained in its full perfection?
Next, [the text] clarifies the meaning of the "sentence on the function" (yòngjù) from below;
then, following that, the Great Master himself explains what the Buddha has already elucidated.
Therefore, in every phrase, the Buddha’s own explanation is first presented;
subsequently, from "Now, the interpretation" onwards, the Great Master’s (Nāgārjuna’s) explanation is clarified.
The intent is to support the Buddha’s explanation, differing from it only in being slightly more extensive.
Regarding the fact that every single phrase states, "In accordance with this intent of the Buddha," the Great Master himself declared:
"I have already set forth the meaning of the Buddha."
He restates the Buddha’s intent to accord with his own view;
"arising" refers to the inverted [perception], which he subsequently explains as being ineffable.
Next, he explains the second phrase, also first citing the sūtra to provide the commentary.
